newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - SAfrican Money targets - By Edward Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - SAfrican Money targets - By Edward Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

Clearly from the monetarist point of view of the Reserve Bank, with money supply growth presently well off even the upper range of the money target, there would appear to be no question of interest rates being reduced.
This does not necessarily follow as an iron law, though, for we have had the experience of the arch practitioners of monetarism, the Bundesbank, doing just that recently.
In April, the Bundesbank reduced rates by a half-point when the money supply growth was 12.2 percent, as against a target range of four to seven percent.
Of course the President of the Bank was able to say "the Bundesbank does not slavishly follow money supply data for one, two or three months, but looks at the basic longer term trend".
There is, accordingly, ample scope for independent discretion for the monetary authorities, which contributes to the mystique of money targeting.

Money targets are set to give notice of the guidelines the authorities will be working with in the fashioning of monetary policy and also to indicate to the private bankers what the monetary authorities expect of them in terms of credit creation.
And yet there is no reason not to expect deviation from them in the short term as economic circumstances dictate.

Nevertheless the targets themselves, at least in South Africa, strain credulity because of the seemingly uncontrollable or wayward expansion of money supply. Targets and actual experience of money growth have emerged as totally independent and unrelated entities.

We are in the eleventh year of money targeting and in the 130 months there have only been 22 months in which the money supply, defined as M3, has been within the target cones and, of that, 14 occured in the downturn and recession years of 1990 and 1992.
This year, 1996, must have been equally frustrating for the authorities. At the time of setting the target in March the preliminary M3 growth for February was relatively low at 12.3 percent.

This is annualised growth from the fourth quarter base of 1995. At this level and with January having been as low as 10.1 percent a target range of six to 10 percent was not only in line with the previous targets but was suitable and realistic as indicating a continued strongly restrictionist monetary policy.

According to the monetarist philosophy permissible monetary growth should accomodate real economic growth, then optimistically expected to be about four percent, and the kind of inflation we should aspire to, say at most six percent.

The Reserve Bank's statutory mandate is, of course, zero inflation, but one must be reasonable. This is, at best, a long term objective. To get there suddenly would be to inflict disastrous deflationary limitations on the economy.

However, M3 growth, instead of moving down towards the target range, continued upwards inexorably to a peak level of 21.1 percent in June, from which it has subsided somewhat, to 17.3 percent, in August, still an awful long way from the upper range.

Clearly the interest rate as the primary instrument of effecting monetary policy has failed and the question to be raised is whether there should be more of the same until it does become effective, or just resign ourselves to its ineffectiveness but continue with the pretence of having such a thing as monetary policy.

This is a dilemma for the Bank; economic considerations militate against an increase in interest rates. On the other hand, to reduce rates, because of the extremely high and punishing real level of interest rates, would give the wrong signal of relaxing monetary policy.

In theory, monetarism entails central bank control of inflation by permitting the money supply to be consistent with real potential economic growth and the target inflation rate. With the central bank controlling money supply, interest rates, prices and economic activity adjust accordingly.

But the Reserve Bank here is unable to have direct control of the money supply - that is largely dictated by the level of credit created by the private banking system - and the Bank therefore seeks to control money demand through the interest rate. Interest rates are expected to influence economic activity and prices and hence money demand.

The interest rate is therefore the fulcrum of monetary policy. Unfortunately money demand in South Africa is proving to be insensitive or unresponsive to interest rates and monetary policy as practised has no real practical power to control.

We are locked into a situation of a continuing strict monetary stance. At best this can be expected to be relaxed as the situation eases. That is the brakes are on all the time but are relaxed only when the car runs out of petrol.

What really needs to be asked is why credit demand continues despite the high level of real interest rates. Part of the answer, unfortunately, is that there is insufficient surplus disposable income for the liquidation of debt and maybe also the payment of interest. In such circumstances credit only accumulates.
This is potentially dangerous for if ever the process is reversed resources will have to be diverted to repay debt, the curse of debt deflation.

It will also be interesting to know how widespread now is the practice of running unit trust schemes in parallel to mortgage bond liabilities for that entails the diversion of resources for the redemption of mortgage liabilities to the inflation of asset values.

The sad fact is that we have got ourselves into a sitaution of permanently high interest rates which we cannot get out of, of our own volition. This has come about because of the unrelenting pursuit of the Holy Grail of zero inflation.
Nor can we escape because of a fear of unleashing inflationary forces.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
